clue.text: Make Bill work in the house?

definitions.text: Make Bill work in the house?

parts.words: Make Bill work in the house?
parts.note: the house is the House of Commons, where a bill is turned into working law; the surface suggests getting someone called Bill to do the chores

explanation.surface: Someone wonders how to get Bill to do the housework.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill is not a man but a parliamentary bill, and the house is Parliament: to make a bill take effect there is to pass it into law.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass legislation into force is the core sense of the verb used of statutes.

clue.text: But does it give a hoot where it swoops?

definitions.text: But does it give a hoot where it swoops?

parts.words: But does it give a hoot where it swoops?
parts.note: 'give a hoot' is the idiom for caring, but here it is meant literally of a large hooting bird of prey that swoops on its quarry

explanation.surface: A sceptic asks whether some careless creature cares where it dives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not give a hoot' means not care; read literally, a hoot is an owl's call, and the swooping predator is the largest owl, named for its eagle-like size.
explanation.definitionFit: This big Eurasian owl hoots and swoops down on prey, matching both halves of the question.

clue.text: Opening account with no lire to exchange causes a banking flap

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only the start of account is used
letters given in exchange are swapped around, so no and lire are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bank charges a fee when a customer opens an account without Italian currency to swap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' gives A from account; 'to exchange' rearranges NO LIRE into ILERON. 'Banking' is about an aircraft tilting in a turn, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: This hinged surface on a wing's trailing edge makes the aircraft roll into a turn, which pilots call banking.

indicators.note: reversing tells us to write the word for role from right to left

parts.note: an actor's role is their part

explanation.surface: A warning that switching roles can be a hazard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversing' turns PART (role) into TRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A snare laid for the unwary is a pitfall, literally a covered pit dug to catch animals.

parts.note: a blackleg is a strike-breaker, also called a scab
a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A sword belonging to a strike-breaking versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackleg is British slang for a worker who breaks a strike.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is what holds a sword or dagger when it is not drawn.

parts.note: what is customary is common, usual
to charm someone is to entrance them

explanation.surface: A test sat with the usual allure.
explanation.walkthrough: COMMON ENTRANCE is the exam British children sit, usually at 13, to enter fee-paying independent schools. 'Entrance' here is the verb meaning bewitch.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a formal test that pupils take for admission to senior private schools in Britain.

definitions.meaning: to inter is to put a body in the ground
a town in Greater Manchester, England

explanation.definitionFit: Burial is interment; and the place is a former mill town near Manchester, the question mark admitting it is a town rather than a city.

parts.note: a musical group is a band
something that is playing is on

explanation.surface: A band performing wildly and freely.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the phrase 'with abandon', meaning with no restraint, so the question mark flags the loose fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild freedom from inhibition is the sense, as in dancing with uninhibited gusto.

definitions.meaning: a Wild West town in Kansas
a sidestep or trick to avoid something

explanation.definitionFit: The Kansas cattle town of Western fame shares its name with a sidestep made to avoid a blow.

clue.text: Naples almost describes this worn-out condition!

definitions.text: Naples almost describes this worn-out condition!

parts.words: Naples almost describes this worn-out condition!
parts.note: read the city's name as nearly 'nap-less', cloth that has lost its raised fibres from wear

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that the Italian city is looking rather shabby.
explanation.walkthrough: Nap is the soft surface pile of fabric; Naples is just one S short of 'napless', fabric worn down to the weave.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth so worn that the weave shows through is shabby, the state of having lost its nap.

clue.text: According to Samuel, he was stone-dead

definitions.text: According to Samuel, he was stone-dead

parts.words: According to Samuel, he was stone-dead
parts.note: the First Book of Samuel tells of a Philistine giant felled by a stone from David's sling

explanation.surface: A biblical report of someone thoroughly dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone-dead' usually means utterly dead; here it means killed by a stone, as the Philistine champion was by David.
explanation.definitionFit: The Philistine giant in 1 Samuel 17 was brought down by a slingshot stone to the forehead.

indicators.note: to switch letters is to swap them about, so a and dimmer are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lighting control needed for a stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switch' rearranges A DIMMER. A dimmer-switch looks like one stage-lighting item. The Mermaid is a theatre in the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The playhouse at Blackfriars in London bears the name of a sea-maiden.

clue.text: Leicester, for example, not entirely primitive

indicators.note: not entirely means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: primitive, early in development

explanation.surface: Someone judges that Leicester is only partly backward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' trims EARLY (primitive) to EARL. Leicester here is not the city but Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, Elizabeth I's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Leicester was a title held by a nobleman, so he is an example of that peerage rank.

indicators.note: bending twists the shape, so the letters of elbow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinker bending the elbow, perhaps not up on the ship's deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bending' rearranges ELBOW. 'Bending the elbow' is slang for drinking, a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, the area under the deck is where you are if not up top.

clue.text: Advantage to have no sun on lakeside grass

indicators.note: to have no sun means the letter for sun is removed from the grass word

parts.note: sedge is a grass-like plant of wet ground

explanation.surface: A grassy shore that is shaded is prized.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to have no' removes S (sun) from SEDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the upper hand or a slight lead over rivals is an advantage.

parts.note: to low is to moo like a cow

explanation.surface: A Low Church procession.
explanation.walkthrough: Low Church is the evangelical wing of the Church of England, a misleading phrase here. Mooch is British slang for an aimless wander.
explanation.definitionFit: An idle stroll with no destination is a saunter, which is what this British slang word means.

parts.note: U is the film classification for universal
to carol is to sing

explanation.surface: A choir rehearsing a carol everyone knows.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the British film certificate meaning suitable for all.
explanation.definitionFit: Employing or putting into effect something is practising it.

parts.note: a light is a window pane
a dressing is a bandage for a wound

explanation.surface: The appeal of a flimsy bandage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' is a noun for a window, not a weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A showy presentation that masks the real substance is the figurative sense of shop display arranging.

parts.note: prim means stiffly proper

indicators.note: set means arranged, so the letters of teas are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A table laid with formal tea for senior clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' rearranges TEAS into ATES after PRIM (formal).
explanation.definitionFit: The senior archbishop of a province holds the title primate, such as the Primate of All England.

clue.text: He drags his feet and trips on a carrot, clumsily

indicators.note: clumsily means awkwardly jumbled, so trips on a carrot are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shuffles along and stumbles over a vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clumsily' rearranges TRIPS ON A CARROT. 'Drags his feet' means delays, not shuffles.
explanation.definitionFit: One who keeps putting tasks off is a delayer, figuratively dragging his feet.

clue.text: Tell the story of dramatic end to election?

definitions.meaning: a second tally of votes demanded when the result is very close

explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to relate events; and a close poll may end with the ballots tallied again.

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
acquires means gets

explanation.surface: A seaman picks up some things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Objects' means aims, not things.
explanation.definitionFit: Objects in the sense of goals or aims are what one sets out to hit.

clue.text: Did Falstaff hit it, taking his nightcap?

definitions.text: Did Falstaff hit it, taking his nightcap?

parts.words: Did Falstaff hit it, taking his nightcap?
parts.note: Shakespeare's Falstaff loved a sherry-like wine; 'hit the' plus the same word is slang for going to bed

explanation.surface: A question about whether Falstaff went to bed after a final drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack was the fortified Spanish wine Falstaff drank in Henry IV; 'hit the sack' means go to bed, and a nightcap is a bedtime drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the old dry white wine Falstaff praised and a slang name for a bed.

clue.text: Spring, when Cardinal left the young lad

indicators.note: left here means departed, so the letter is taken away

parts.note: N, north, is one of the cardinal points of the compass

explanation.surface: In springtime a cardinal departed, leaving a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' removes N (a cardinal point) from SPRING. Cardinal seems to be a churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned word for a youth is a sprig, a young offshoot of a family.

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: Something got going, as in the time of a ban.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts EG inside BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: To have commenced something is to have started it.

parts.note: a T-square, so T stands for square
a rim is an edge

explanation.surface: A slice with a straight border.
explanation.walkthrough: T is a crossword convention for square, from the draughtsman's T-square.
explanation.definitionFit: To clip or shorten neatly is to trim.

clue.text: Woman is quiet in this part of the Strand, we hear

parts.note: P, piano, is the musical sign for quiet

explanation.surface: A woman keeps silent in a district of London's Strand.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a London street, but here strand means a thread of hair; 'we hear' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin wisp of hair is a single strand or fine piece of it.

clue.text: Novel bit of a problem, mathematically

indicators.note: bit of means a short run of letters is taken from inside the phrase

explanation.surface: A small part of a maths problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit of' takes EMMA from problEM MAthematically. It is Jane Austen's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's 1815 novel bears its heroine's first name.

indicators.note: inside means these pieces go into the track word

parts.note: a track or way is a route

explanation.surface: Formula One drivers named on a race track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts I and N (name) inside ROUTE. 'Formula I' looks like motor racing.
explanation.definitionFit: A set procedure followed every time is a fixed formula.

clue.text: How French to make a remark!

explanation.definitionFit: It is the French interrogative 'how?'; and in English it is the verb for passing an observation.

parts.note: from 'between you, me and the' post at a field entrance, a secret shared with a standing post

explanation.surface: An honest person one can trust with secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright' suggests honest, but means a standing post; the saying 'between you, me and the ...' makes it the confidant.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright post hung with a gate is the third party in a well-known saying about secrets.

definitions.meaning: the pons asinorum, a proposition in Euclid called the bridge of these animals

explanation.definitionFit: Donkeys stand for fools; and Euclid's fifth proposition is called the pons asinorum, the bridge of donkeys.
